data.content_ref: inline:exp-hist:{"target": "14a2cc3cf1e82b1c87d845c4057062a9d71b2939504587febb42398d05f25f45", "seq": 1, "objection": "The target's analogy fails because it conflates the descriptive mechanism of biological survival with the normative justification required for scientific preference. While natural selection explains why organisms survive retrospectively without implying future success, Popper's problem addresses why scientists are *rationally justified* in preferring one theory over another for future action. The target claims preference is merely a 'survival trait' of the community, but this dissolves the normative force of the preference into a sociological fact. If preference is only an evolutionary adaptation and not grounded in any logical relation to truth or verisimilitude (which the target explicitly dismisses), then acting on the 'fittest' theory is no more rational than acting on any other surviving trait; it renders the scientist's choice arbitrary from the perspective of seeking truth, thereby smuggling in an unjustified assumption that evolutionary survival correlates with future predictive success—a form of induction by another name.", "outcome": "raised and not answered; the target's status did not move"}
